::: {.lead}
Think about yesterday. Maybe you sent a voice message, paid a bill on your
phone, or filled in a form on the university website. All of these are
*digital skills*. Today almost every job asks for them, too. But many people
only say "I am good with computers". That is not clear. In this lab session
you learn what digital skills are, how a European list puts them in groups,
and why employers need them. You also make your own skills profile on the lab
computer.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary digital-skills digital-literacy digital-competence digcomp competence-area proficiency-level labour-market lifelong-learning >}}

## 1.1 Skills, literacy and competence

We use three words in this course. Each word is bigger than the one before
(@fig-circles).

![Skills, literacy and competence. Each one contains the one before.](images/skills-circles.png){#fig-circles width=66%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — Skills, literacy and competence"}
**Digital skills** are what you can *do* with a device: send an e-mail, save
a file, fill in a form. **Digital literacy** adds *understanding*: you check
if information is true before you share it. **Digital competence** adds good
*behaviour*: you use digital tools safely and responsibly.
:::

Here is the difference. Ahmad types very fast. But he gives his password to
his friends. Ahmad has good skills, but he is not yet digitally competent.

We also talk about three levels (@tbl-levels).

| Level | What the person does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| basic | uses a phone and common apps | sends an e-mail, fills in an online form |
| intermediate | uses apps well at work | makes a chart in a spreadsheet |
| advanced | builds and runs technology | writes programs, runs a network |

: Three levels of digital skills. {#tbl-levels}

Most jobs need the basic and the intermediate level in many apps. This course
teaches exactly these levels.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — One day of an office assistant"}
Mona works as an office assistant in a small company. In one day she:

1. signs in to her work e-mail with a password and a code on her phone;
2. answers the e-mails of customers;
3. writes a letter in a word processor and saves it as a PDF;
4. puts the orders of the day in a spreadsheet.

Mona does not write programs. But every task is a digital skill.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Your digital week"}
1. Write five things you did on a computer or a phone this week (for
   example "sent a voice message" or "paid a bill").
2. Next to each one, write its level: basic, intermediate or advanced.

*Your result:* a list of five tasks with their levels.
:::

## 1.2 DigComp: five areas of digital skills

"Good with computers" can mean many things. So the European Union made a list
of the digital skills that every person needs. Its name is **DigComp**. It puts
the skills in **five areas** (@fig-digcomp).

![The five areas of DigComp.](images/digcomp-areas.png){#fig-digcomp width=96%}

| Area | In simple words | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Information and data | find, check and keep information | checking if a news story is true |
| 2 Communication and collaboration | talk and work with others online | writing a polite message to a teacher |
| 3 Digital content creation | make documents, photos and videos | writing a CV in a word processor |
| 4 Safety | protect your device, your data and your health | using a screen lock on your phone |
| 5 Problem solving | fix small problems, learn new apps | finding out why the printer does not print |

: The five areas of DigComp. {#tbl-digcomp}

DigComp also has **levels**: how well a person can do a task. The levels are
in four groups (@fig-levels-ds).

![The DigComp levels in four groups.](images/proficiency.png){#fig-levels-ds width=84%}

| Group | Levels | The person … |
|---|---|---|
| foundation | 1–2 | does simple tasks with help |
| intermediate | 3–4 | does normal tasks alone |
| advanced | 5–6 | does many kinds of tasks and helps others |
| highly specialised | 7–8 | solves hard problems and leads others |

: The four groups of levels. {#tbl-bands}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — Daily tasks in DigComp"}
Which area is each task in?

1. You check if a message about free phones is true: **information and data**.
2. You send your homework to your teacher with a short, polite note:
   **communication and collaboration**.
3. You make a birthday card with a photo: **digital content creation**.
4. You cannot make a chart yet, so you watch a short online lesson:
   **problem solving**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Digital skills means programming." No. Programming is only one small part of
DigComp. You can be very good at digital skills without writing any code.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Your DigComp profile"}
1. Open the **DigComp self-check** below on the lab computer (or scan its QR
   code with your phone).
2. For each skill, choose the level that is true for you. Your answers stay
   in this browser only.
3. Find your strongest area and your weakest area.
4. Save your profile as a PDF. You need it in the next lab session.

*Your result:* your profile, and one goal for your weakest area.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/digcomp-check.html" poster="sims/digcomp-check.png" title="DigComp self-check" height="760" >}}

## 1.3 Why every job needs digital skills

The **labour market** is the place where people look for work and employers
look for workers. Today digital skills are important there, for three
reasons.

1. **Almost every job is digital.** Shops, banks, schools and offices all use
   computers and phones.
2. **Computers do the simple, repeated tasks.** People must use the computer
   programs and check their work.
3. **Apps change often.** A worker must learn new apps many times.

So employers like workers who can learn a new app alone. They also like
workers who keep learning during their whole working life. We call this
**lifelong learning**.

![Every job uses digital tools.](images/jobs.png){#fig-studio width=92%}

| Job | Digital tasks | DigComp areas |
|---|---|---|
| shop assistant | prices on the computer, card payments, online orders | 1, 4 |
| bank clerk | online forms, customer e-mails, safe passwords | 2, 4 |
| office assistant | letters, spreadsheets, shared folders | 3, 1, 2 |
| teacher | online lessons, marks in a spreadsheet, messages to parents | 2, 1 |

: Digital tasks in common jobs. {#tbl-roles}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.3 — Reading a job advert"}
A company looks for a "Receptionist". The advert says: *"answer e-mails from
customers; keep the visitor list in a spreadsheet; make simple posters; keep
customer data private."*

1. Answering e-mails: area 2 (communication).
2. The visitor list in a spreadsheet: area 1 (information and data).
3. Simple posters: area 3 (content creation).
4. Keeping customer data private: area 4 (safety).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · A real job advert"}
1. On a job website, find one real job advert in your field of study.
2. Copy three of its requirements into a document.
3. Next to each requirement, write its DigComp area.
4. Save the document with the name `job-advert.docx`.

*Your result:* three requirements with their areas.
:::

## Case study: hiring at Sunrise Company

*Sunrise Company* is a made-up company with an office and a shop. It needs
two new workers: an office assistant and a sales assistant. The office
assistant answers the e-mails of customers. The sales assistant makes short
videos about new products. Every worker signs in with a code on the phone.
The company reads what each person can do in each DigComp area.

The mini-game below is the hiring desk of Sunrise Company. You put each task
of the job adverts in its DigComp area. Then you read what the people say
about their level, and you choose the right person.

## Further reading

Evans, Martin and Poatsy, *Technology in Action*, 18th ed., Chapter 1;
European Commission, *DigComp 2.2: The Digital Competence Framework for
Citizens*, 2022.

## Exercises

1. What is the difference between digital skills and digital competence?
2. Write the names of the five DigComp areas.
3. Which DigComp area is each task in? (a) updating the apps on your phone;
   (b) putting your photos in folders; (c) making a short video;
   (d) learning a new app from an online lesson.
4. A student can send a file only when a friend helps. Which group of levels
   is this?
5. Why must workers keep learning new apps?
6. Choose one job from @tbl-roles. Write two of its digital tasks.
7. *Sunrise Company*: the sales assistant makes short videos. Which DigComp
   area is this?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Skills are what you can do; competence adds safe and responsible behaviour.
2. Information and data; communication and collaboration; digital content creation; safety; problem solving.
3. (a) safety; (b) information and data; (c) digital content creation; (d) problem solving.
4. Foundation (levels 1–2).
5. Apps change often, and computers take over simple tasks.
6. For example, teacher: online lessons, marks in a spreadsheet.
7. Digital content creation.
:::
